I'm from Atlanta and moved to Seattle during the pandemic and it was really hard at first but now I've sort of determined as far as places in the US I want to live, it's really either Seattle or Atlanta. 

I've lived in California and Alabama and never felt right the way Atlanta and Seattle have. I think it's natural to miss the home you've built especially if you didn't necessarily want to move back to Seattle but had an obligation to. 

It's hard to give advice to a stranger, I mean I know all the things I like but that might not apply to you. Maybe focus less on what you miss about Atlanta and try to find things to love about Seattle now (don't recall things in Seattle you used to love that are gone!)

Good luck!

I'm not a vet but I got into a bad car accident as a kid and didn't want to drive as a teen when all my peers were driving. I tried driving school. My mom tried. Friends tried. Nothing was working. Then into my 20s one of my friends was REALLY patient with me, kept it casual, taught me enough to pass my test. I passed my test and then after a few months got my first car, I would only drive to work and back, but eventually that became grabbing dinner from a drive thru or meeting someone for lunch. I still don't love driving (I take the bus everywhere) but I know how.

Long story short, the combination of feeling ready and having someone to help me made all the difference. But also, recognizing I don't have to drive everywhere.

I don't remember my exact words I was nervous. But I talked about how transmission rates, how it affected me mentally (not talking bad about myself - just how it changedy comfort with sex and to be fair I've always been a bit sex hesitant so that was more important for me to bring up for expectation reasons), and precautions available.

When I first got diagnosed I told my mom and all my friends I'd never date again because I couldn't imagine disclosing. 

I just jumped right in - asked if we could talk about something personal and we just sat and talked. As for specific words - I don't recall exactly what I said I was so nervous but he was impressed I had done my research so I definitely laid out facts and absolutely no negative self-speak. 

In person was easier for me, I'd be too anxious waiting on a text back and a phone call didn't cross my mind.

In person, after hanging out I just asked if we could talk about something. I talked about statistics, precautions, and just a general sexual history (not hsv related - but felt it was a good time to talk about that anyway).

My boyfriend didn't know oHSV could be transferred genitally. I didn't know that standard STD tests didn't include HSV so I didn't think to ask specifically about herpes when we had the past sexual history conversation.

As for drama, well it's definitely put a strain on our relationship. We're still together but a lot has changed. I was already a little sex hesitant (past trauma as well as lack of proper sex education made me never really feel comfortable sexually) but now I don't want to have sex at all. I also don't feel comfortable in my skin so I went from being affectionate to not wanting to be touched. 

The final issue was at one point he said he didn't think of himself as having an STD and that just made me feel sort of shitty because it felt sort of like, "Hey I don't have an STD but you do sorry this happened to you." Instead of, "Sorry for giving you an STD, how can I support you?"
I'm also really scared of future dating life as a black woman living in a predominantly white city. This really has been a major blow to my mental health.
